prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect, and its experimental discovery in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: B044 remains my first choice after reading all eight opening ballots. It is the only shortlisted candidate with six rankers, four top-three placements and a theory-and-experiment pair that maps onto the credited names: Kane and Mele for the Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall proposal, Molenkamp for the observation of helical edge transport in HgTe/CdTe wells. It fits the committee's 'discovery or invention' test as I understand it (the committee identifies the topic and the people responsible for the original work, not a lifetime of achievement), because the prediction, the material realisation and the measured signature are each concrete and independently reproduced over nearly two decades in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and, through the three-dimensional extension, in Bi-based compounds. The consequences for materials physics are broad: spectroscopic, transport and microscopy groups use the edge and surface states as routine probes. Recognition is timely to overdue rather than premature.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The HgTe/CdTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang was what made Molenkamp's experiment possible, and the three-dimensional topological insulator contributors (Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others) are outside the credited strings, so a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize would leave visible omissions and the committee would need to defend that boundary. A second concern, raised by several colleagues, is that the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and phases of matter already honoured the topological theme, so the committee may see this as a follow-on rather than a new subject. I judge the quantum spin Hall effect to be a distinct, experimentally established phenomenon, but the objection is legitimate.

responses.point: Ranks B044 first as a clean prediction followed by a decisive experiment, but flags that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and Moore make allocation a real question.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific assessment and with the allocation worry. Where I would go further is on the experimental side: the Molenkamp result is not a routine confirmation, since the HgTe edge-channel conductance quantisation was the first direct evidence that the predicted state exists, and I would not let the BHZ omission remove it from the prize. If the committee cannot resolve the theory credit, I would rather keep the Kane-Mele core intact and say so in the citation than redefine the topic to fit a different set of names.

responses.point: Ranks B037 (dynamical mean-field theory) first as a standard non-perturbative framework, and B044 second, noting that the 2016 topological prize left this strand unrecognised.
responses.response: I share your view that the 2016 prize did not cover time-reversal-invariant topological insulators, which is why I weigh the overlap objection lightly. I am less persuaded on B037. DMFT is enormously useful, but it is a method and framework whose early credit (Metzner, Muller-Hartmann) lies outside the credited names, and you yourself flag that the framing is delicate. Against the 'discovery or invention' criterion I find it harder to point to a single originating discovery than for the spin Hall state, where a theoretical prediction and a measured phenomenon can be cited.

responses.point: Ranks B024 (optical lattice clocks) first as a concrete, clearly defined invention, and places B044 third while stressing that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are missing and the 2016 prize may reduce appetite.
responses.response: I take the clocks seriously: it is the cleanest two-name credit on the shortlist and I ranked it sixth mainly because of proximity to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, not for lack of merit. Our difference is on the 2016 point. The 2016 citation concerned topological phase transitions and topological phases in matter (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz); the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall effect were not what was recognised, and a significant observed phenomenon followed. I accept your point that the missing BHZ names make B044 less tidy than B024, and I would keep B024 as an alternative if the committee cannot agree on B044's boundaries.

responses.point: Ranks B024 first because better measurement opens new physics, and ranks B044 fifth while deferring to colleagues because it lies outside his specialism.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour about specialism, and I would note that on B044 the experimental evidence is unusually accessible: quantised edge conductance in HgTe wells and later ARPES on Bi-based materials are the type of measured result you favour for lattice clocks. I do not read the lattice clock as merely an engineering refinement, but unlike B044 it is a continuation of a line already recognised in 2005 and 2012, which for me is the main reason it sits behind the topological candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can defend a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp configuration without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, or whether the omission would be seen as an unfair cut.
How much weight the 2016 topological-phases prize should carry against a prize for the Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall effect.
I rely on general knowledge for the priority chronology of the Kane-Mele and BHZ papers and of the early HgTe transport measurements, and have not independently verified it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B044, B020 or B024. My TEM and interface work (including oxide interfaces) is methodologically adjacent to some candidates but I have no documented collaboration with any credited person. Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, but his top-ranked candidate (B042) is not part of my preferred configuration and nothing in my profile suggests a conflict.
